summary: Tonbo makes camera-like equipment that helps organisations see and observe, including devices that form pictures from heat. It also supplies parts that other equipment makers build into their products.
description: A normal camera forms a picture using light. Thermal-imaging equipment detects heat energy given off by objects and turns differences into an image. Tonbo combines sensors, electronics and software to make observation devices or parts for a larger machine, such as a vehicle’s vision system.
money: Customers pay for equipment, parts and agreed design or fitting work. Tonbo must pay engineers, buy components, arrange production, test products and provide promised support. The amount billed is different from the profit left after these and other costs.
customers: Armed forces, police and other security agencies in India and abroad buy equipment for their users. Other defence equipment makers buy Tonbo parts to put inside their own equipment. In the offer document, a large share of recent sales came from exports, especially to Europe. The organisation paying Tonbo may therefore be different from the person who eventually uses the finished device.
drivers: Winning firm orders, getting the required parts, completing tests, delivering working equipment and receiving customer payment. A delayed order or a problem with an important component can hold up several stages.

groups.title: Devices that help users observe
groups.examples: Finished thermal cameras and sights, including sights used to aim weapons from military vehicles.
groups.explanation: The customer buys a working device rather than a bag of electronic parts. Its sensors collect signals, software turns them into images, and the finished equipment must pass the checks agreed with the buyer.

groups.title: Vision equipment fitted to vehicles
groups.examples: Driver-vision and surroundings-viewing systems in the land-products catalogue.
groups.explanation: Think of a customer wanting a driver to see around a vehicle in difficult viewing conditions. The equipment must fit and work with that vehicle; designing and testing the fit can be part of the job.

groups.title: Parts for other equipment makers
groups.examples: Imaging modules, processing boards and related components.
groups.explanation: A module is a smaller working unit built into a larger product. Another manufacturer can buy Tonbo’s imaging unit and combine it with its own equipment. Tonbo receives payment for its part, not automatically the price of the whole machine.

groups.title: Designing equipment to work together
groups.examples: Combined sensing systems, plus newer defence systems listed on its website such as a drone interceptor.
groups.explanation: Some customers need several pieces of equipment and software to work as a system. Agreeing the design, building it and showing that it works can take longer than selling a standard device.

basics.title: A technical demonstration is not yet a sale
basics.text: Showing a possible customer that a device works is an early step. The buyer still has to place an order, agree the terms and receive equipment that meets the contract.

basics.title: Testing is part of the product
basics.text: An institutional buyer can require checks before approving a design or accepting a delivery. If a part changes or a test fails, engineers may have to do more work before the customer accepts the equipment.

steps.title: Find out what the buyer needs
steps.text: Agree what the equipment must do, where it will be fitted and how the buyer will check it.

steps.title: Design and arrange the parts
steps.text: Engineers select components, develop the software and arrange how the equipment will be made.

steps.title: Build, test and deliver
steps.text: Make or assemble the agreed equipment and complete the required checks. A delivery may still need the buyer’s approval.

steps.title: Get approval, bill and collect
steps.text: Send the bill under the contract and collect payment when due. Tonbo must fund engineering and parts while waiting, and carry out any support it has promised.

specifics.title: A promised opportunity can disappear
specifics.text: An enquiry or invitation to bid is not a firm purchase. Even a confirmed order still needs delivery and acceptance. Read what stage the company’s announced opportunities have actually reached.

specifics.title: A small part can delay a finished device
specifics.text: An unavailable sensor or electronic component can hold up assembly. Replacing it may require redesign and new tests, adding cost even when customers still want the product.

specifics.title: Special design work needs to earn its cost back
specifics.text: A customised system may require engineering work that a standard repeat order does not. More sophisticated equipment does not automatically leave more profit after design, testing and support.

watch: Which possible orders have become firm purchases?
A demonstration or enquiry does not oblige a buyer to pay.
Look for confirmed contracts, what is to be supplied and the delivery conditions. Keep possible future opportunities separate from orders the customer has actually committed to.
Are delivered devices being accepted and paid for?
Equipment can leave the factory before customer payment arrives.
Read how the customer approves a delivery and when a bill becomes due. Compare unpaid customer bills, called receivables, with cash generated by running the business.
Does the business rely heavily on a few buyers?
An important customer can delay or reduce an entire programme of purchases.
Look for how much business comes from major customers and whether orders repeat. Read delivery dates and cancellation terms rather than assuming government demand arrives evenly throughout the year.
Can parts and production keep up with orders?
The right component has to be available and pass the buyer’s requirements.
Read supplier dependence, imported parts, production arrangements and delays. Extra manufacturing capacity is useful only if the company can obtain parts and supply equipment the buyer accepts.
Are new designs leading to paying customers?
Engineering and support cost money before a product proves successful.

Look for actual orders and repeat deliveries after a launch. Check spending on development and promised repairs or support; a new technology announcement alone does not show that those costs have been recovered.
risks: Customer budgets, bidding and approval procedures can delay purchases and payment.
Losing or delaying a large order can leave staff and materials waiting for work.
Shortages, failed checks and redesign can raise costs or delay delivery.
Export rules, customer permissions and promised after-sale work can restrict sales or add expenses.
context: Tonbo’s share sale paid existing owners, not the company

Tonbo’s shares began trading on NSE on 23 October 2026. The whole offer was an offer for sale: existing shareholders sold some of their shares to new investors. The prospectus states that Tonbo itself receives none of that money, so the listing does not pay for new factories, parts or research. Its engineering, parts and production must still be paid for from customer payments or other funding. Separately, a finished device may attract more attention, but another manufacturer can keep ordering the imaging unit inside its own equipment; check which route brings repeat purchases.
quiz: If a customer likes a demonstration, has Tonbo already earned a sale?
No. The customer must agree a purchase, and Tonbo must meet the contract’s delivery and approval conditions. Cash arrives according to the payment terms.
